shared.title: How the Printing Press Spread Literacy
shared.text:
Before the middle of the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, usually by trained scribes. Producing a single book could take months, so books were rare and expensive, and reading was a skill largely limited to the clergy and the wealthy. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg, a German goldsmith, developed a printing press that used movable metal type. Individual letters could be arranged into pages, inked, pressed onto paper, and then reused for new pages.

The new technology spread with remarkable speed. By 1500, print shops were operating in more than two hundred European cities, and together they had produced millions of books. Because a printer could make hundreds of identical copies in the time a scribe needed for one, the price of books fell sharply. Printers also published more and more works in everyday languages such as German, French, and English rather than only in Latin, which most people could not read.

Cheaper books did not make people literate overnight; in many regions, most adults still could not read two centuries later. However, the press created a steady supply of affordable reading material, from religious texts to almanacs and pamphlets. This supply gave ordinary families a practical reason to learn to read and made schooling more valuable. In this sense, the printing press did not teach anyone to read, but it changed what reading could offer.

shared.title: Requesting a book through interlibrary loan

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Hi, I need a book for my history paper, but the catalog says our library doesn't have it.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Okay. If we don't own a book, you can request it through interlibrary loan. We borrow it from another university's library for you.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Oh, I've never done that. Is it expensive?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: It's free for students. You just fill out a short form online with your student login. A book usually takes one to two weeks to get here, though.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Two weeks? My paper's due in ten days.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Hmm. Do you need the whole book, or just a chapter or two?

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Really just one chapter, the one about early trade routes.

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Then I'd request a scanned copy of that chapter instead. Scans usually come by email in three or four days.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: That's perfect. Is there a limit on scans?

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: Because of copyright rules, it's one chapter per book. And if you ever borrow a physical book this way, you get it for three weeks. You can only renew it if the lending library agrees.

lines.speaker: Woman
lines.text: Got it. I'll submit the chapter request right now. Thanks so much!

lines.speaker: Man
lines.text: You're welcome. You'll get an email as soon as it's ready.

shared.question: Some universities let students decide for themselves whether to attend lectures, as long as they pass the exams. Others require attendance and lower the grades of students who miss too many classes. Should universities require class attendance? Why or why not?

posts.name: Maya
posts.text: I think attendance should be required. When I know my attendance counts, I go to every class, and I learn much more from the discussions than from reading the slides alone. Professors also explain what will be on the exam during class. Without a rule, many students would skip and then fall behind.

posts.name: Daniel
posts.text: I disagree with required attendance. University students are adults, and many of us work part-time jobs or care for family members. If someone can learn the material from recorded lectures and the textbook, they should be judged on what they know, not on whether they sat in a classroom.
